title: An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding
author: David Hume
openingChapterLabel: Section 1 — Of the Different Species of Philosophy
openingText: Moral philosophy, or the science of human nature, can be approached in two different ways, each with its own merit, and each capable of contributing to the entertainment, instruction, and reform of mankind. The first considers man chiefly as a being born for action, guided in his choices by taste and feeling, pursuing one object and avoiding another according to the value those objects seem to have and the light in which they appear. Since virtue, of all objects, is granted to be the most valuable, philosophers of this kind paint her in the most attractive colors, drawing every resource from poetry and eloquence and treating their subject in an easy, accessible way best suited to please the imagination and engage the affections.
about:
Hume wrote the Enquiry as a deliberate second attempt. His first book, A Treatise of Human Nature, had appeared anonymously in 1739–40, when he was twenty-eight, and had — in his own later words — 'fallen dead-born from the press.' He blamed the failure on the manner of presentation rather than the doctrine, and in 1748 he reissued the core of the Treatise's first book in a shorter, sharper, more accessible form as the Philosophical Essays Concerning Human Understanding, retitled An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding in 1758. He continued to revise it through the rest of his life; the authorized text is the posthumous edition of 1777. The Enquiry is the book Hume wanted to be judged by.

The argument is consecutive. Section 1 defends 'abstruse' philosophy against its critics. Section 2 lays down the empiricist principle that every genuine idea is a copy of some prior impression. Section 3 sketches how ideas associate. Sections 4 and 5 contain what is now usually called the problem of induction: the demonstration that no chain of reasoning, demonstrative or probable, can carry us from past observed regularities to a single future case, and the 'sceptical solution' that we get there anyway by custom or habit. Section 7 analyses the idea of necessary connexion and concludes that what we call causation is, in the objects, nothing more than regular succession; the felt necessity is in the mind. Section 8 applies the same analysis to liberty and necessity and produces the classical compatibilist position. Section 10 is the argument against believing reports of miracles. Sections 11 and 12 turn the empiricist instrument on natural theology and on philosophy itself, and end with the famous instruction to commit any volume of divinity or school metaphysics to the flames.

It is the most consequential book of British empiricism. Kant said in the Preface to the Prolegomena that Hume's suggestion 'first interrupted my dogmatic slumber' and gave his investigations in speculative philosophy a new direction; the Critique of Pure Reason is in large part an attempt to answer the questions the Enquiry posed. Bentham, Mill, the logical positivists, and the twentieth-century philosophy of science all worked downstream of it. Modern debates over induction, causation, free will, and the epistemology of testimony still take Hume as the canonical statement of the problem. The book is short, ferociously clear, and reads like a man taking the apparatus of human reason apart on the table to see exactly what each piece does.

angleCards.title: The problem of induction.
angleCards.text: Sections 4 and 5 are the most famous argument in the book. Hume shows that no reasoning — demonstrative or probable — can carry the mind from past regularities to a single future case. The sun has risen every day; nothing in logic guarantees it will rise tomorrow. Read carefully and notice what survives the demolition.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the argument of Sections 4 and 5 in detail — what Hume claims about reason, what he concedes to custom or habit, and whether the 'sceptical solution' actually solves anything.

angleCards.title: Causation as constant conjunction.
angleCards.text: Section 7 dismantles the idea of necessary connexion. When one billiard ball strikes another, what do the senses actually deliver? Succession, contiguity, regularity — but never a perceived bond. The necessity, Hume argues, is something the mind adds. Watch the argument move from the table to the head.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Hume's analysis of cause and effect closely — what he claims is in the objects, what he claims is in the mind, and what is left of causation by the end of Section 7.

angleCards.title: Miracles and testimony.
angleCards.text: Section 10 is the most explosive single chapter in eighteenth-century philosophy. Hume gives a rule for weighing testimony against the laws of nature it would have to overturn, and concludes that no testimony has ever been sufficient to establish a miracle as the foundation of a religion. The argument has been attacked ever since. Read it on its own terms first.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Section 10 in full — Hume's general maxim about testimony, his four practical objections, and decide whether the argument lands as cleanly as he thinks it does.

angleCards.title: The empiricist standard.
angleCards.text: The closing pages tell the reader exactly what to do with any book that fails the Enquiry's test. Does it contain abstract reasoning about quantity or number? Does it contain experimental reasoning about matter of fact? If not, commit it to the flames. Notice that Hume applies the rule to his own discipline and not just to his opponents.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Sections 11 and 12 as the book's own self-application — the empiricist principle turned on natural theology, on metaphysics, and on philosophy itself.

cast.name: David Hume
cast.description: Scottish philosopher (1711–1776), born in Edinburgh, trained in law but driven by what he called 'an insurmountable aversion to everything but the pursuits of Philosophy and general Learning.' He wrote the Treatise in France in his twenties, was disappointed by its reception, and recast its first book as the Enquiry a decade later. He spent his life in private scholarship, diplomatic posts, and the writing of his enormously successful History of England. Twice denied a university chair for suspicion of irreligion. He revised the Enquiry through every edition he lived to see.

cast.name: Impressions and Ideas
cast.description: Hume's basic distinction, laid down in Section 2. Impressions are the lively perceptions present when we feel, see, hate, love, will. Ideas are the fainter copies the mind makes from impressions when it thinks or remembers. The whole book turns on a single test: every genuine idea must be traceable to some prior impression, and any term that cannot be traced is, in Hume's word, suspect. The test is the empiricist instrument the rest of the Enquiry uses on causation, necessity, the self, and God.

cast.name: Relations of Ideas and Matters of Fact
cast.description: Hume's other foundational distinction, opening Section 4. Relations of ideas — geometry, algebra, arithmetic — are intuitively or demonstratively certain; their truth depends on nothing in the world. Matters of fact — that the sun will rise, that fire burns — are never demonstrable; their contrary can always be coherently imagined. The whole problem of induction follows from putting causal reasoning on the second side of the line. Twentieth-century logical positivists called the same distinction analytic and synthetic and built much of their programme on it.

cast.name: Custom or Habit
cast.description: Once Hume has shown that no reasoning carries the mind from observed regularities to expectations about the future, he is left with the question of why the mind makes the inference anyway. His answer, in Section 5, is custom or habit. Not a faculty of reason but a propensity built up by repeated exposure. Custom is the great guide of human life. It is also, on Hume's account, what we have instead of the rational foundation we cannot have.

cast.name: Necessary Connexion
cast.description: The target of Section 7. When one event regularly follows another, ordinary language says the first causes the second and that there is a necessary tie between them. Hume runs the empiricist test on the idea of necessity and finds no impression that corresponds to it in the objects. What corresponds to it is the felt determination of the mind to pass from the impression of one event to the idea of its usual companion. Causation, on this analysis, is regular succession plus a habit of expectation. The position has been argued about ever since.

cast.name: The Argument Against Miracles
cast.description: Hume's most controversial single argument. A miracle is a violation of a law of nature; a law of nature is established by a uniform experience; the only evidence for a miracle is testimony; therefore the proof against any miracle is, from the nature of the case, as complete as any proof from experience can be. Testimony establishes a miracle only when the falsehood of the testimony would itself be more miraculous than the event it reports. Hume thinks no historical case has ever met that bar. The argument has been the centre of debate over the rationality of religious belief from his own time to the present.

acclaim.quote: I openly confess, the suggestion of David Hume was the very thing, which many years ago first interrupted my dogmatic slumber, and gave my investigations in the field of speculative philosophy quite a new direction.
acclaim.context: Preface to the Prolegomena to Any Future Metaphysics, 1783

acclaim.quote: David Hume is one of the most important among philosophers, because he developed to its logical conclusion the empirical philosophy of Locke and Berkeley, and by making it self-consistent made it incredible.
acclaim.context: A History of Western Philosophy, Book III, Chapter XVII, 1945

acclaim.quote: The type of critical reasoning which was required for the discovery of this central point was decisively furthered, in my case, especially by the reading of David Hume's and Ernst Mach's philosophical writings.
acclaim.context: Autobiographical Notes, in Albert Einstein: Philosopher-Scientist, ed. P. A. Schilpp, 1949

whyItMatters.title: The Problem of Induction
whyItMatters.body: Sections 4 and 5 isolate a difficulty no philosophy has yet disposed of. We expect the future to resemble the past — that bread will nourish, that fire will burn, that the sun will rise — and we run our lives on those expectations. Hume asks what justifies them. Not demonstration: the contrary of every matter of fact is coherently imaginable, so no contradiction follows from supposing the sun will not rise tomorrow. Not probable reasoning either, because every probable argument from past to future already assumes the uniformity it is supposed to establish, and the assumption is the thing in question. Hume's conclusion is that the inference is not the work of reason at all but of custom or habit — a propensity of the mind, not a discovery of logic. The argument has been attacked, dressed up, formalised, and reframed by Popper, Goodman, and the Bayesians, but the original problem keeps coming back. Anyone who has tried to write a foundation for machine-learning generalisation has run into Hume's question in modern dress.

whyItMatters.title: Causation Without Necessity
whyItMatters.body: Section 7 takes the idea of necessary connexion and runs it through the empiricist test. When two billiard balls collide, what does experience actually deliver? Contiguity, succession, and regularity, repeated as often as one likes. What it does not deliver is a perceived tie, a felt 'must,' a glimpse of the force by which one event compels the next. Hume concludes that necessity is not in the objects but in the mind — a determination, built up by custom, to expect the one upon seeing the other. The analysis was scandalous in its time and has been the starting point of philosophical work on causation ever since. Russell took it to its limit and proposed dispensing with the notion of cause altogether. Contemporary work on causal inference in statistics and machine learning still negotiates the gap Hume opened between regular succession and genuine causation.

whyItMatters.title: The Argument Against Miracles
whyItMatters.body: Section 10 is the single most consequential chapter of eighteenth-century philosophy of religion. Hume sets a general rule for testimony: no report should be believed when its falsehood would be less miraculous than the event it reports. He then argues, in Part 2, that no historical testimony has ever cleared that bar — not because of any special hostility to religion but because the testimony in every famous case fails on internal grounds that he lays out one by one. The argument has been answered, refined, and re-attacked continuously from Paley to Earman, and the form of the debate has barely changed. The Enquiry is also the book that Kant credited with waking him from his 'dogmatic slumber'; the Critique of Pure Reason is, in large part, an attempt to answer the same questions Hume's empiricism left open. Any modern argument about the rationality of testimony — courtroom evidence, eyewitness reports, the credibility of unusual claims online — is working in the conceptual space Hume mapped.
